newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl feels left in lurch by employers - union boss.
newsitem.headline: Kohl feels left in lurch by employers - union boss.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl feels he has been left in the lurch by German employers after pushing through a package to cut labour costs and will try to soothe relations with workers at a trade union conference, a union leader said.

Roland Issen, leader of the DAG white-collar trade union, told Sunday's edition of the Bild am Sonntag newspaper he had held a private meeting with the chancellor in September to discuss Kohl's appearance at the union's congress this month.

The chancellor's bold bid to enter the lion's den comes at a time when relations between government and unions have cooled considerably after his coalition passed a law last month allowing employers to cut employees' sick pay.

Over 120,000 workers across Germany walked out on Tuesday in protest at the measures, part of an austerity drive to shape up for Europe's planned single currency and slash wage costs which companies say make them uncompetitive in world markets.

"We're now seeing the first signs that the chancellor has recognised this confrontation course is the wrong one," Issen told the paper. "He's obviously realising more and more that the employers... have left him in the lurch."

The unions have repeatedly accused employers of playing on fears Germany lags behind in the global marketplace to persuade Bonn to abandon Germany's consenus-based social market economy and move to a form of capitalism with fewer social benefits.

Many of Germany's biggest companies, such as Daimler-Benz, have set about implementing the cuts immediately, provoking the ire of unions who say the changes cannot be incorporated into existing wage contracts.
"The fact that the unions haven't just gone back to their daily business after the sick-pay law is also giving (Kohl) pause for thought," Issen said.
A government spokesman confirmed the talks between Kohl and Issen had taken place.
Although he declined to discuss their content, they appear to tally with an impression that all sides are ready to talk about their differences after months of stubborn stalemate.
Germany's biggest union, IG Metall, said on Saturday its leaders would meet the engineering employers group Gesamtmetall on Monday for the first time since the law was passed.
The law allows employers to pay 80 percent of full wages as sick pay instead of the previous 100 percent.
"The current problems can't be solved by confrontation. We can only solve them together," Egon Schaefer, the deputy leader of the IG Chemie union, told Bild am Sonntag.
